title: Τηλέμαχος ἐς ἄστυ
about: At dawn Telemachus ties on his sandals, takes his spear and tells the swineherd that he is going to the town, so that his mother may see him at last; the swineherd is to bring the beggar along later. The beggar, who is Odysseus, agrees, and says he will come when he has warmed himself. Telemachus walks to the house, where the old nurse sees him first and Penelope, weeping, throws her arms round him and asks how he fared. He tells her only to wash, pray and promise sacrifices, and goes out to the assembly. Athena has given him a wondrous grace, and the suitors crowd round him with fair words and evil thoughts, but he sits with his father's old companions. Peiraeus brings the stranger who sailed with Telemachus and offers to send the gifts Menelaus gave; Telemachus puts the offer off, since he cannot yet tell how matters with the suitors will end. The two guests are then bathed and fed in the house, and Penelope begins to speak.

sentences.t:
ἦμος δ’ ἠριγένεια φάνη ῥοδοδάκτυλος Ἠώς,
δὴ τότ’ ἔπειθ’ ὑπὸ ποσσὶν ἐδήσατο καλὰ πέδιλα
Τηλέμαχος, φίλος υἱὸς Ὀδυσσῆος θείοιο,
sentences.l:
When early-born appeared, rose-fingered Dawn,
then indeed, thereupon, under his feet he bound fair sandals,
Telemachus, dear son of Odysseus, divine,
sentences.i: When early-born Dawn appeared, rose-fingered, then Telemachus, the dear son of divine Odysseus, bound his fair sandals under his feet,
sentences.n: ἦμος … δὴ τότε is a pair, 'when … then': the dawn clause comes first and δὴ τότε (with ἔπειθ’, 'thereupon') picks up the main action. Line 1 is the standing dawn line, in which ἠριγένεια 'early-born' and ῥοδοδάκτυλος 'rose-fingered' are both epithets of Dawn and are translated every time. ποσσίν is a dative plural in -σσι(ν); ἐδήσατο is the aorist middle of δέω 'bind', 'bound on for himself'. θείοιο is a genitive in -οιο (Attic θείου).

sentences.t:
εἵλετο δ’ ἄλκιμον ἔγχος, ὅ οἱ παλάμηφιν ἀρήρει,
ἄστυδε ἱέμενος, καὶ ἑὸν προσέειπε συβώτην·
sentences.l:
and he took up a sturdy spear, which to his palm was fitted,
townward pressing, and his own addressed swineherd:
sentences.i: and took up his sturdy spear, which fitted his hand, and, eager to be off to the town, spoke to his own swineherd:
sentences.n: ἄλκιμον 'sturdy' comes from ἀλκή 'might' and is the epithet of this spear; ἔγχος is 'spear'. ὅ οἱ is 'which … to him' and παλάμηφιν has the suffix -φιν, 'in/at the palm'. ἀρήρει is the pluperfect of ἀραρίσκω 'fit', 'had been fitted' and so 'fitted'. ἄστυδε has the direction suffix -δε, 'to the town'. ἑόν is the possessive 'his own' (not the relative), and συβώτης 'swineherd' is a compound of σῦς 'pig' and the root of βόσκω 'feed'; προσέειπε 'addressed' introduces the speech.

sentences.t:
ἄττ’, ἦ τοι μὲν ἐγὼν εἶμ’ ἐς πόλιν, ὄφρα με μήτηρ
ὄψεται·
sentences.l:
“Father, indeed I for my part am going to the town, so that me my mother
may see;
sentences.i: “Father, I am going to the town, so that my mother may see me;
sentences.n: ἄττα (elided ἄττ’) is a courteous address to an older man, 'father', and implies no family tie: Telemachus is speaking to the swineherd. ἦ τοι μέν 'indeed … for my part' sets his own errand against the one he gives the swineherd in the next sentences. εἶμι has future sense, 'I am going'. ἐγών is ἐγώ with a final ν. ὄφρα … ὄψεται is a purpose clause; ὄψεται may be read as a future indicative or as a subjunctive with a short vowel (= ὄψηται).

sentences.t:
οὐ γάρ μιν πρόσθεν παύσεσθαι ὀΐω
κλαυθμοῦ τε στυγεροῖο γόοιό τε δακρυόεντος,
πρίν γ’ αὐτόν με ἴδηται·
sentences.i: for I do not think she will stop her hateful weeping and tearful lamentation before she has seen me myself;
sentences.n: ὀΐω 'I think' takes the future infinitive παύσεσθαι, 'that she will cease', with μιν 'her' as its subject, and the genitives κλαυθμοῦ and γόοιο say what she will cease from. στυγεροῖο and δακρυόεντος are genitives, the first in -οιο, and δακρυόεις 'tearful' is 'full of tears'. πρίν γε … ἴδηται is 'until she sees', with the subjunctive and no κε; αὐτὸν με is 'me in person'.

sentences.t: ἀτὰρ σοί γ’ ὧδ’ ἐπιτέλλω.
sentences.l: but to you, for your part, thus I give charge.
sentences.i: But this is what I charge you to do.
sentences.n: ἀτάρ 'but, and now' turns from his own plan to the swineherd's task. ὧδε 'thus' points forward to the instruction that follows at once, so the full stop here is a pause and not an end of thought. ἐπιτέλλω 'lay a charge on, enjoin' takes the dative σοί; the same verb comes back in line 21 as ἐπιτειλαμένῳ, in Odysseus' mouth. σοί γε is 'to you at least', 'for your part'.

sentences.t:
τὸν ξεῖνον δύστηνον ἄγ’ ἐς πόλιν, ὄφρ’ ἂν ἐκεῖθι
δαῖτα πτωχεύῃ·
sentences.l:
The stranger, the wretched one, lead to the town, so that there
a meal he may beg;
sentences.i: Take the wretched stranger to the town, so that he may beg a meal there;
sentences.n: Read ἄγ’ as ἄγε, the imperative of ἄγω 'lead', and not as the exclamation 'come!': the object is τὸν ξεῖνον δύστηνον. τόν is the old demonstrative 'that', so 'the stranger there', and the stranger is the beggar who is to go into town. δύστηνος 'wretched' is translated each time. ὄφρ’ ἂν … πτωχεύῃ is a purpose clause with ἄν and the subjunctive. ἐκεῖθι 'there' is built with the place suffix -θι. πτωχεύω 'beg, live as a beggar' takes δαῖτα 'a meal' as object.

sentences.t:
δώσει δέ οἱ ὅς κ’ ἐθέλῃσι
πύρνον καὶ κοτύλην·
sentences.l:
and will give him whoever may wish
a wheaten loaf and a cup;
sentences.i: and whoever wishes will give him a wheaten loaf and a cup;
sentences.n: δώσει is the future of δίδωμι, and its subject is the relative clause ὅς κ’ ἐθέλῃσι, 'whoever may wish': the indefinite relative takes κε and the subjunctive, here with the old ending -σι (= ἐθέλῃ). οἱ is 'to him'. πύρνος is a wheaten loaf (the word is built on πυρός 'wheat') and κοτύλη is a cup or small measure; the Greek does not say what is in the cup.

sentences.t:
ἐμὲ δ’ οὔ πως ἔστιν ἅπαντας
ἀνθρώπους ἀνέχεσθαι, ἔχοντά περ ἄλγεα θυμῷ·
sentences.l:
but for me not at all is it possible all
men to put up with, having indeed pains in my heart;
sentences.i: but I cannot at all put up with every man, beset as I am by pains in my heart;
sentences.n: ἔστιν with its first syllable accented means 'it is possible', and ἐμέ … ἔχοντα is the accusative subject of the infinitive ἀνέχεσθαι 'to put up with', so 'it is not possible for me to bear'. ἅπαντας ἀνθρώπους is 'all men'. In ἔχοντά περ ἄλγεα θυμῷ the particle περ stresses the participle, 'having pains in my heart' (i: 'beset … by pains'); with a participle περ can also mean 'although', but the sense here is that his own pain leaves no room for the rest. ἄλγεα is 'pains'.

sentences.t:
ὁ ξεῖνος δ’ εἴ περ μάλα μηνίει, ἄλγιον αὐτῷ
ἔσσεται·
sentences.l:
and the stranger, even if he is very angry, more painful for him
it will be;
sentences.i: and if the stranger is very angry, it will be the more painful for him;
sentences.n: ὁ ξεῖνος is 'that stranger', the beggar again, and εἴ περ is 'even if'. μηνίει is from μηνίω 'be angry, bear a grudge'. ἄλγιον is the comparative of the adjective that goes with ἄλγος 'pain', 'more painful', so it picks up ἄλγεα in the line before; αὐτῷ 'for him' is the dative of the person who suffers, the stranger himself. ἔσσεται is ἔσται with doubled σ. ἔσσεται, which opens line 15, is the verb that completes the clause begun in line 14.

sentences.t: ἦ γὰρ ἐμοὶ φίλ’ ἀληθέα μυθήσασθαι.
sentences.l: for indeed to me dear, true things, to speak.”
sentences.i: for to speak the truth is dear to me.”
sentences.n: ἦ γάρ is 'for truly'. φίλ’ is a neuter plural, 'dear things', and ἀληθέα 'true' is the uncontracted neuter plural (Attic ἀληθῆ); with ἐστί understood, the infinitive μυθήσασθαι 'to say' is the subject, so 'telling true things is dear to me'. The aorist of μυθέομαι means 'speak, tell'. With this line Telemachus' speech to the swineherd ends.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη πολύμητις Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.l: Him answering addressed many-wiled Odysseus:
sentences.i: In answer Odysseus of many wiles said to him:
sentences.n: This is the standing line for an answer given in reply. ἀπαμειβόμενος 'answering' goes with προσέφη 'addressed', and πολύμητις 'of many wiles' is Odysseus' epithet (μῆτις is cunning intelligence). The line names the speaker: the 'stranger' of Telemachus' speech, the beggar, is Odysseus, and he is the one who now answers.

sentences.t: ὦ φίλος, οὐδέ τοι αὐτὸς ἐρύκεσθαι μενεαίνω·
sentences.l: “O friend, nor I myself, you know, am eager to be held back;
sentences.i: “Friend, I myself have no wish to be kept back either;
sentences.n: ὦ φίλος is 'O friend', a friendly address, with the nominative φίλος doing duty as a vocative. οὐδέ … αὐτός is 'nor … I myself', and τοι is the enclitic 'to you', an appeal to the listener, 'you know'. μενεαίνω with an infinitive means 'be eager', and ἐρύκεσθαι is the passive of ἐρύκω 'hold back, keep', so 'to be kept back, detained'. Telemachus has just told the swineherd to take him into town, and Odysseus agrees: he has no wish to be kept at the farm.

sentences.t:
πτωχῷ βέλτερόν ἐστι κατὰ πτόλιν ἠὲ κατ’ ἀγροὺς
δαῖτα πτωχεύειν·
sentences.l:
For a beggar better is it through the town than through the fields
a meal to beg;
sentences.i: It is better for a beggar to beg his meal in the town than out in the country;
sentences.n: βέλτερον 'better' is the comparative of ἀγαθός, and ἠέ is 'than' after it. πτωχῷ is the dative 'for a beggar'. κατά with the accusative here means 'about, through'. πτόλιν is an old form of πόλιν, which Telemachus used in line 6; both forms stand in this passage. πτωχεύειν is an infinitive that stands as the subject of ἐστί, and δαῖτα 'a meal' is its object.

sentences.t: δώσει δέ μοι ὅς κ’ ἐθέλῃσιν.
sentences.l: and will give to me whoever may wish.
sentences.i: and whoever wishes will give to me.
sentences.n: Odysseus takes Telemachus' own words from line 11, δώσει δέ οἱ ὅς κ’ ἐθέλῃσι, and changes only οἱ 'to him' to μοι 'to me' and adds a movable ν to ἐθέλῃσιν. The construction is as there: ὅς κε with the subjunctive, 'whoever may wish'. The English repeats the earlier clause, as the Greek does.

sentences.t:
οὐ γὰρ ἐπὶ σταθμοῖσι μένειν ἔτι τηλίκος εἰμί,
ὥστ’ ἐπιτειλαμένῳ σημάντορι πάντα πιθέσθαι.
sentences.l:
for not at the steadings to stay any longer of such an age am I,
as, to an overseer having given charge, to obey in everything.
sentences.i: for I am no longer of an age to stay on at the steading and do everything I am told once an overseer has given his orders.
sentences.n: οὐ … ἔτι is 'no longer'. σταθμοῖσι is a dative plural in -οισι; a σταθμός is a standing place, here a farm steading. τηλίκος 'of such an age' is completed by ὥστε with the infinitive πιθέσθαι 'to obey', aorist middle of πείθομαι. ἐπιτειλαμένῳ is the aorist middle participle of ἐπιτέλλω, the verb of line 9, agreeing with the dative σημάντορι, 'to an overseer', the person obeyed after πιθέσθαι; σημάντωρ is 'one who gives the signal', 'overseer, commander', from σημαίνω.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἔρχευ·
sentences.l: But go;
sentences.i: But go on;
sentences.n: ἔρχευ is the imperative of ἔρχομαι 'go' in its Ionic shape (Attic ἔρχου). ἀλλά here is 'well then, but', turning from what he does not want to what he will do. The phrase is a whole sentence, and the ano teleia after it is a real pause before he says how he will follow.

sentences.t:
ἐμὲ δ’ ἄξει ἀνὴρ ὅδε, τὸν σὺ κελεύεις,
αὐτίκ’ ἐπεί κε πυρὸς θερέω ἀλέη τε γένηται.
sentences.l:
and me will lead this man here, whom you bid,
at once, when of the fire I am warmed and warmth has come about.
sentences.i: and this man here, whom you bid, will lead me as soon as I have been warmed at the fire and the warmth has come.
sentences.n: ἀνὴρ ὅδε 'this man here' is the swineherd, and τὸν σὺ κελεύεις 'whom you bid' refers back to ἄγ’ in line 10. ἄξει is the future of ἄγω. θερέω is the aorist passive subjunctive (1 sg.) of θέρομαι 'get warm', uncontracted (the contracted form would be θερῶ), and πυρός is a genitive of the source of the warmth. ἐπεί κε … γένηται is 'as soon as … has come about'; ἀλέη is 'warmth'.

sentences.t: αἰνῶς γὰρ τάδε εἵματ’ ἔχω κακά·
sentences.l: for terribly these clothes I have, bad;
sentences.i: for these clothes of mine are terribly bad;
sentences.n: αἰνῶς is an adverb from αἰνός 'dreadful', so 'dreadfully', and it goes with κακά 'bad'. εἵματα is the plural of εἷμα 'garment', 'clothes', and τάδε 'these here' points to the rags he is wearing. ἔχω 'I have' is here 'I wear'. The γάρ explains why he wants to wait by the fire.

sentences.t:
μή με δαμάσσῃ
στίβη ὑπηοίη·
sentences.l:
lest me overpower
the frost of dawn;
sentences.i: lest the frost of early morning overpower me;
sentences.n: μή with the subjunctive δαμάσσῃ expresses fear, 'lest it overpower me'; the verb is δαμάζω 'subdue, master'. στίβη is 'frost, hoar-frost'. ὑπηοίη 'of the dawn, early' is built on ὑπό and ἠώς 'dawn', and agrees with στίβη; line 1 has set the scene at dawn.

sentences.t: ἕκαθεν δέ τε ἄστυ φάτ’ εἶναι.
sentences.l: and far off, he said, the town is.”
sentences.i: and the town, he said, is far off.”
sentences.n: ἕκαθεν has the suffix -θεν 'from', literally 'from afar', and is used for 'far off'. δέ τε adds the epic τε to δέ. φάτ’ is φάτο elided, the unaugmented imperfect middle 3 sg. of φημί (= ἔφατο), 'he said', with ἄστυ … εἶναι as its accusative and infinitive. Another parse of the elided form is φάτε 'you (pl.) said', which would need Telemachus and the swineherd together as the speakers. The Greek does not say who said it, and this part shows no such remark, so the English leaves it as 'he'. ἄστυ is 'town', the same word as ἄστυδε in line 5. With this the beggar's speech ends.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάτο, Τηλέμαχος δὲ διὰ σταθμοῖο βεβήκει,
κραιπνὰ ποσὶ προβιβάς, κακὰ δὲ μνηστῆρσι φύτευεν.
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and Telemachus through the steading had gone,
at a rush with his feet striding forward, and evils for the suitors he was planting.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and Telemachus went out through the steading, striding forward at a rush and devising evil for the suitors.
sentences.n: ὣς φάτο is the formula 'so he spoke' (φάτο = ἔφατο, no augment). βεβήκει is a pluperfect with the sense of a state reached, 'was on his way'. σταθμοῖο is a genitive in -οιο, and διά with the genitive is 'through'. κραιπνά is a neuter plural used as an adverb, 'at a rush'; προβιβάς is the participle of προβιβάω (προβίβημι) 'stride forward' (προ- and a reduplicated present of βαίνω). φύτευεν is the imperfect of φυτεύω 'plant': the poet says Telemachus was planting harm for the suitors (l 'planting', i 'devising evil'), and Telemachus uses the verb himself in line 82.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεί ῥ’ ἵκανε δόμους εὖ ναιετάοντας,
ἔγχος μέν ῥ’ ἔστησε φέρων πρὸς κίονα μακρήν,
αὐτὸς δ’ εἴσω ἴεν καὶ ὑπέρβη λάϊνον οὐδόν.
sentences.l:
But when he reached the well-inhabited house,
his spear, then, he stood, carrying it, against a tall pillar,
and he himself went inside and stepped over the stone threshold.
sentences.i: When he reached the well-inhabited house, he carried his spear to a tall pillar and stood it against it, then went inside himself and stepped over the stone threshold.
sentences.n: δόμους εὖ ναιετάοντας 'the well-inhabited house' is a formula; the plural δόμους is used for a single dwelling, and ναιετάω 'dwell' makes the house one that is well lived in. ἵκανε is the imperfect of ἱκάνω 'reach'. ἔστησε is the transitive aorist of ἵστημι, 'made stand'. ῥ’ is the particle ῥα 'then'. ἴεν is the imperfect of εἶμι 'went', and ὑπέρβη the aorist of ὑπερβαίνω 'step over', both without augment; λάϊνον is 'of stone'.

sentences.t:
τὸν δὲ πολὺ πρώτη εἶδε τροφὸς Εὐρύκλεια,
κώεα καστορνῦσα θρόνοις ἔνι δαιδαλέοισι,
δακρύσασα δ’ ἔπειτ’ ἰθὺς κίεν·
sentences.i: The nurse Eurycleia saw him first by far, as she was spreading fleeces on the finely wrought chairs, and, bursting into tears, went straight to him;
sentences.n: τροφός is the nurse who brought him up. πολὺ πρώτη is 'first by far'. κώεα 'fleeces' (sheepskins) lie on the seats. καστορνῦσα is κατά (shortened to κα- before στ-) with στορνῦσα, a participle of στόρνυμι 'spread', and θρόνοις ἔνι has ἔνι for ἐνί after its noun, 'on chairs'. δαιδαλέοισι 'wrought' means skilfully worked. δακρύσασα is the aorist participle 'having burst into tears'; ἰθύς 'straight' and κίεν, an unaugmented imperfect of κίω, say that she made for him directly.

sentences.t:
ἀμφὶ δ’ ἄρ’ ἄλλαι
δμῳαὶ Ὀδυσσῆος ταλασίφρονος ἠγερέθοντο,
καὶ κύνεον ἀγαπαζόμεναι κεφαλήν τε καὶ ὤμους.
sentences.l:
and around him others,
maidservants of Odysseus enduring-minded, gathered,
and kissed him, gladly welcoming, both head and shoulders.
sentences.i: and the other maids of steadfast Odysseus gathered round him, and welcomed him gladly, kissing his head and shoulders.
sentences.n: ἀμφὶ … ἠγερέθοντο is 'gathered round', with ἀμφί standing apart from its verb, and ἠγερέθοντο is an epic form of ἀγείρομαι 'assemble'. δμῳαί are the house's maidservants, and ἄλλαι 'others' sets them beside Eurycleia. ταλασίφρων 'enduring-minded', Odysseus' epithet, is translated every time, and here marks the women as his. κύνεον is an imperfect of κυνέω 'kiss', without augment; ἀγαπαζόμεναι is 'welcoming gladly'; κεφαλήν and ὤμους are the objects of κύνεον.

sentences.t:
ἡ δ’ ἴεν ἐκ θαλάμοιο περίφρων Πηνελόπεια,
Ἀρτέμιδι ἰκέλη ἠὲ χρυσέῃ Ἀφροδίτῃ,
sentences.l:
And she came out of her chamber, circumspect Penelope,
like to Artemis or golden Aphrodite,
sentences.i: Then circumspect Penelope came out of her chamber, like Artemis or golden Aphrodite,
sentences.n: ἡ δ’ is 'and she', the article as a pronoun. ἴεν is the imperfect of εἶμι 'went', and θαλάμοιο a genitive in -οιο, 'out of the chamber'. περίφρων Πηνελόπεια is her stock name-phrase, 'circumspect Penelope'. ἰκέλη 'like' takes the dative, here Ἀρτέμιδι and Ἀφροδίτῃ, and χρυσέῃ 'golden' is the epithet of Aphrodite. She is likened to the goddesses for her beauty, as she appears before her son.

sentences.t:
ἀμφὶ δὲ παιδὶ φίλῳ βάλε πήχεε δακρύσασα,
κύσσε δέ μιν κεφαλήν τε καὶ ἄμφω φάεα καλά,
καί ῥ’ ὀλοφυρομένη ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.l:
and about her dear child she threw her arms, having wept,
and kissed him on the head and on both fair eyes,
and, lamenting, winged words she spoke:
sentences.i: and, weeping, she threw her arms about her dear son, and kissed him on his head and on both his fair eyes, and, lamenting, spoke winged words:
sentences.n: ἀμφὶ … βάλε is 'threw about', with ἀμφί apart from its verb, and πήχεε is a dual, 'her two arms'. παιδὶ φίλῳ is 'her dear child', in the dative. κύσσε is the aorist of κυνέω 'kiss', and φάεα καλά 'fair lights' is the plural of φάος used for the eyes; she calls him φάος in the next line. ὀλοφυρομένη means 'lamenting'. The last line is the formula 'she spoke winged words', in which ἔπεα πτερόεντα is rendered the same each time.

sentences.t: ἦλθες, Τηλέμαχε, γλυκερὸν φάος.
sentences.l: “You have come, Telemachus, sweet light.
sentences.i: “You have come, Telemachus, my sweet light.
sentences.n: φάος 'light' is what one cannot do without, and calling a person 'light' is an endearment; γλυκερόν is 'sweet'. The neuter noun is in apposition to the masculine name, in the vocative. ἦλθες is a plain aorist and is better rendered 'you have come'. The word φάος is the singular of the φάεα she has just kissed, in line 39.

sentences.t:
οὔ σ’ ἔτ’ ἐγώ γε
ὄψεσθαι ἐφάμην, ἐπεὶ ᾤχεο νηῒ Πύλονδε
λάθρη, ἐμεῦ ἀέκητι, φίλου μετὰ πατρὸς ἀκουήν.
sentences.l:
Not you any more I, at least,
thought to see, since you were gone by ship to Pylos
in secret, against my will, in quest of news of your dear father.
sentences.i: I did not think I should see you again, since you had gone off by ship to Pylos, in secret, against my will, in search of news of your dear father.
sentences.n: οὔ … ἔτι is 'no longer', and ἐφάμην 'I said to myself, thought' takes the future infinitive ὄψεσθαι. ᾤχεο is the 2nd sg. imperfect of οἴχομαι 'be gone' with the augment lengthened (Attic ᾤχου), and νηῒ is the dative of ναῦς; Πύλονδε has the direction suffix -δε. ἐμεῦ is the Ionic ἐμοῦ, and ἀέκητι with the genitive means 'against the wish of'. μετά with the accusative ἀκουήν 'news' is 'in pursuit of', so 'in quest of news of', and φίλου πατρός is 'your dear father'.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἄγε μοι κατάλεξον ὅπως ἤντησας ὀπωπῆς.
sentences.l: But come, recount to me how you came upon the sight.”
sentences.i: But come now, tell me how you came to see it.”
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἄγε is 'but come', where ἄγε is an exclamation that opens a request; it is the same form as the imperative ἄγ’ 'lead' in line 10, but not the same use. κατάλεξον is the aorist imperative of καταλέγω 'recount in full'. ὅπως 'how' opens an indirect question. ἤντησας is the aorist of ἀντάω 'meet', which takes the genitive: ὀπωπῆς 'a sight'. The Greek gives ὀπωπῆς no owner: it is the sight he came upon on his journey, and the English leaves it unnamed.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ αὖ Τηλέμαχος πεπνυμένος ἀντίον ηὔδα·
sentences.l: To her in turn prudent Telemachus spoke, face to face:
sentences.i: Then prudent Telemachus spoke to her in turn, face to face:
sentences.n: A standing reply-formula: τὴν δ’ αὖ is 'and her in turn', and ἀντίον ηὔδα 'spoke facing her' says that he spoke straight to her. Telemachus' epithet πεπνυμένος 'prudent' is translated every time he is named in this formula. The pronoun τήν is feminine: in line 77 the same line comes with τόν for Peiraeus.

sentences.t:
μῆτερ ἐμή, μή μοι γόον ὄρνυθι μηδέ μοι ἦτορ
ἐν στήθεσσιν ὄρινε φυγόντι περ αἰπὺν ὄλεθρον·
sentences.l:
“Mother mine, not for me lamentation rouse, nor for me the heart
in my breast stir up, indeed having escaped steep destruction;
sentences.i: “Mother, do not rouse lamentation in me, or stir up the heart in my breast, now that I have escaped steep destruction;
sentences.n: μή with the present imperatives ὄρνυθι (from ὄρνυμι 'rouse') and ὄρινε (from ὀρίνω 'stir') is a prohibition, and μοι is the dative 'in me', 'for me'. στήθεσσιν is a dative plural in -εσσι(ν). φυγόντι agrees with μοι, 'to me who have escaped'; περ stresses it, 'indeed escaped', where περ with a participle can instead mean 'although'. αἰπὺν ὄλεθρον 'steep destruction' is rendered by the house phrase.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὑδρηναμένη, καθαρὰ χροῒ εἵμαθ’ ἑλοῦσα,
εἰς ὑπερῷ’ ἀναβᾶσα σὺν ἀμφιπόλοισι γυναιξὶν
εὔχεο πᾶσι θεοῖσι τεληέσσας ἑκατόμβας
ῥέξειν, αἴ κέ ποθι Ζεὺς ἄντιτα ἔργα τελέσσῃ.
sentences.l:
but having washed, and taken clean garments for your skin,
having gone up to the upper chamber with your attendant women,
pray to all the gods, complete hecatombs
to offer, if ever Zeus deeds of requital should accomplish.
sentences.i: But wash yourself, put on clean clothing, go up to your upper room with your attendant women, and pray to all the gods, promising to offer complete hecatombs if Zeus should ever bring deeds of requital to pass.
sentences.n: The sentence is one command: the participles ὑδρηναμένη, ἑλοῦσα and ἀναβᾶσα are all subordinate to εὔχεο 'pray'. εὔχομαι with the future infinitive ῥέξειν is 'pray (promising) to perform', a vow. τεληέσσας ἑκατόμβας are 'complete hecatombs'. ἄντιτα ἔργα is rendered 'deeds of requital' (ἄντιτος is built on ἀντί 'in return' and the root of τίνω 'pay'; whether it means 'requiting' or 'requited' is not certain), and τελέσσῃ 'bring to completion' has the same root as τεληέσσας. αἴ κέ ποθι is 'if ever' with the subjunctive.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐγὼν ἀγορὴν ἐσελεύσομαι, ὄφρα καλέσσω
ξεῖνον, ὅτις μοι κεῖθεν ἅμ’ ἕσπετο δεῦρο κιόντι.
sentences.l:
but I to the assembly shall go, so that I may call
the stranger, who from there with me followed here, as I came.
sentences.i: But I shall go to the assembly to call the stranger who followed me here from there when I came.
sentences.n: αὐτάρ 'but' sets his own errand against what he has told her to do. ἀγορήν is an accusative of the place to which, with no preposition, so 'to the assembly'. ἐσελεύσομαι is the future of εἰσέρχομαι. ὄφρα … καλέσσω is a purpose clause. ὅτις is 'who, whoever', and the dative μοι … κιόντι is 'to me coming': the stranger followed him as he came. κεῖθεν 'from there' has the suffix -θεν; ἕσπετο is the aorist of ἕπομαι 'follow'.

sentences.t:
τὸν μὲν ἐγὼ προὔπεμψα σὺν ἀντιθέοις ἑτάροισι,
Πείραιον δέ μιν ἠνώγεα προτὶ οἶκον ἄγοντα
ἐνδυκέως φιλέειν καὶ τιέμεν, εἰς ὅ κεν ἔλθω.
sentences.l:
Him, on the one hand, I sent ahead with godlike companions,
and Peiraeus I had bidden, him to his house leading,
kindly to befriend and to honour, until I come.”
sentences.i: I sent him ahead with my godlike companions, and I had told Peiraeus to take him to his house, treat him as a friend, kindly, and honour him until I come.”
sentences.n: Peiraeus is a man's name: he has a house (line 75) and is told to look after the stranger. τὸν μέν … Πείραιον δέ sets the two against each other. προὔπεμψα is προ + ἔπεμψα with the vowels run together, 'sent ahead'; ἀντιθέοις is 'godlike'. ἠνώγεα is a pluperfect of ἄνωγα 'I command' that serves as a past tense, 'I bade' (English says 'I had bidden' because the bidding came before this speech), and μιν 'him' is the object of ἄγοντα. φιλέειν and τιέμεν are infinitives (the second in -έμεν) that depend on ἠνώγεα. εἰς ὅ κεν ἔλθω is 'until I come'.

sentences.t: ὣς ἄρ’ ἐφώνησεν, τῇ δ’ ἄπτερος ἔπλετο μῦθος.
sentences.l: So then he spoke, and to her wingless was the speech.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and for her the speech was wingless.
sentences.n: ἄπτερος 'wingless' turns the formula ἔπεα πτερόεντα 'winged words' (line 40) upside down. The Greek does not say whose speech is meant (τῇ is 'to her' or 'for her'); the line may mean that she made no answer, so that no winged words went back. The translation keeps the literal picture and does not decide. ἐφώνησεν is the aorist of φωνέω 'speak', and ἔπλετο is the aorist of πέλομαι 'be, become'; τῇ is the pronoun 'to her'.

sentences.t:
ἡ δ’ ὑδρηναμένη, καθαρὰ χροῒ εἵμαθ’ ἑλοῦσα,
εὔχετο πᾶσι θεοῖσι τεληέσσας ἑκατόμβας
ῥέξειν, αἴ κέ ποθι Ζεὺς ἄντιτα ἔργα τελέσσῃ.
sentences.l:
And she, having washed, and taken clean garments for her skin,
prayed to all the gods, complete hecatombs
to offer, if ever Zeus deeds of requital should accomplish.
sentences.i: She washed, put on clean clothing, and prayed to all the gods, promising to offer complete hecatombs if Zeus should ever bring deeds of requital to pass.
sentences.n: Penelope does what her son has told her: line 58 is line 48 with ἡ δ’ in place of ἀλλ’, and lines 59 and 60 are lines 50 and 51 with εὔχετο, the imperfect, for the imperative εὔχεο. The going up of line 49 is not repeated. ὑδρηναμένη is an aorist participle of ὑδραίνομαι 'wash oneself', and the English repeats the earlier wording where the Greek repeats; the exact sense of ἄντιτα is uncertain, as said at line 51.

sentences.t:
Τηλέμαχος δ’ ἄρ’ ἔπειτα διὲκ μεγάροιο βεβήκει
ἔγχος ἔχων·
sentences.l:
And Telemachus then through the hall had gone out,
holding his spear;
sentences.i: Then Telemachus went out through the hall, holding his spear;
sentences.n: διέκ is διά and ἐκ together, 'out through', and μεγάροιο is a genitive in -οιο. βεβήκει is the pluperfect again, 'was on his way'. Telemachus has taken up again the spear that he left standing by the pillar in line 29; the poet does not say so. ἔγχος ἔχων 'holding his spear' keeps ἔγχος as 'spear'.

sentences.t: ἅμα τῷ γε δύω κύνες ἀργοὶ ἕποντο.
sentences.l: together with him two swift dogs followed.
sentences.i: two swift dogs followed along with him.
sentences.n: κύνες ἀργοί is the house phrase 'swift dogs', and ἀργός can mean 'swift' or 'white' (the meaning is disputed, and 'swift' is the house choice). δύω is δύο 'two'. τῷ γε is 'him', the article as a pronoun, in a dative that goes with ἅμα 'together with'. ἕποντο is the imperfect of ἕπομαι 'follow'.

sentences.t: θεσπεσίην δ’ ἄρα τῷ γε χάριν κατέχευεν Ἀθήνη·
sentences.l: And wondrous upon him a grace poured-down Athena.
sentences.i: And Athena shed a wondrous grace upon him.
sentences.n: θεσπεσίην is 'wondrous', and χάριν 'grace' is the charm that makes onlookers stare. κατέχευεν is the aorist of καταχέω 'pour down'; Athena makes him look wonderful to the people. τῷ γε is 'upon him'. The next line tells what the grace does.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἄρα πάντες λαοὶ ἐπερχόμενον θηεῦντο.
sentences.l: And at him all the people, as he came on, were marvelling;
sentences.i: All the people gazed at him in wonder as he came;
sentences.n: τὸν is 'him', the object of θηεῦντο, the imperfect of θηέομαι 'gaze at in wonder' in its contracted Ionic shape. ἐπερχόμενον 'as he came on' agrees with τόν. λαοί are the people at large, not the suitors, who are named in the next line. This line is the result of Athena's gift in the line before.

sentences.t:
ἀμφὶ δέ μιν μνηστῆρες ἀγήνορες ἠγερέθοντο
ἔσθλ’ ἀγορεύοντες, κακὰ δὲ φρεσὶ βυσσοδόμευον.
sentences.l:
And around him the lordly suitors gathered,
good things speaking, but evils in their minds they were plotting in the depths.
sentences.i: The lordly suitors gathered round him, speaking good things, while in the depths of their minds they plotted evil.
sentences.n: μνηστῆρες ἀγήνορες is rendered 'the lordly suitors' each time. ἔσθλ’ is ἐσθλά 'good things', set against κακά 'evils' by the δέ of the line (there is no μέν): kind words, evil thoughts. φρεσί is the dative plural of φρήν 'mind'. βυσσοδόμευον is an imperfect of βυσσοδομεύω, a compound of βυσσός 'depth' and a verb of building, so 'plot in the depths'. Compare the narrator's κακά in line 27.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὁ τῶν μὲν ἔπειτα ἀλεύατο πουλὺν ὅμιλον,
ἀλλ’ ἵνα Μέντωρ ἧστο καὶ Ἄντιφος ἠδ’ Ἁλιθέρσης,
οἵ τε οἱ ἐξ ἀρχῆς πατρώϊοι ἦσαν ἑταῖροι,
ἔνθα καθέζετ’ ἰών·
sentences.l:
but he, of these, then avoided the great throng,
and to where Mentor sat, and Antiphus, and Halitherses,
who for him from the beginning his father’s own companions were,
there he sat down, having gone;
sentences.i: But he avoided the great throng of them, and went and sat where Mentor sat, and Antiphus, and Halitherses, who from the beginning had been companions of his father’s day;
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ὁ is 'but he'. τῶν μέν is 'of them' with πουλὺν ὅμιλον 'the great throng' (πουλύς = πολύς), and the contrast is ἀλλά 'but instead'. ἵνα is the relative adverb 'where', answered by ἔνθα 'there'; it does not mean 'in order that'. ἧστο is from ἧμαι 'sit'. πατρώϊοι ἑταῖροι is 'companions of his father's day'. καθέζετ’ ἰών is 'sat down, having gone'.

sentences.t: τοὶ δ’ ἐξερέεινον ἕκαστα.
sentences.l: and they questioned him about each thing.
sentences.i: and they asked him about every detail.
sentences.n: τοί is the old plural of the article used as 'they', here the three men beside whom he has sat down. ἐξερέεινον is the imperfect of ἐξερεείνω 'question closely, ask out', and ἕκαστα is 'each thing', a neuter plural.

sentences.t:
τοῖσι δὲ Πείραιος δουρικλυτὸς ἐγγύθεν ἦλθεν
ξεῖνον ἄγων ἀγορήνδε διὰ πτόλιν·
sentences.l:
And to them Peiraeus, famed-for-the-spear, from close by came,
the stranger leading to the assembly through the town;
sentences.i: And Peiraeus, famed for his spear, came up to them from close by, bringing the stranger through the town to the assembly;
sentences.n: δουρικλυτός 'famed-for-the-spear' is a compound of δόρυ 'spear' (in the stem δουρ-) and κλυτός 'famed'. ἐγγύθεν has the suffix -θεν 'from', 'from close by'. τοῖσι is a dative plural in -οισι, 'to them', the group already seated. ἄγων 'leading' is a participle whose object is ξεῖνον; ἀγορήνδε has the direction suffix -δε, 'to the assembly', and πτόλιν is the old form of πόλιν.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ἄρ’ ἔτι δὴν
Τηλέμαχος ξείνοιο ἑκὰς τράπετ’, ἀλλὰ παρέστη.
sentences.l:
and not then for long any more
Telemachus away from the stranger turned, but stood beside him.
sentences.i: And Telemachus did not for long keep away from the stranger, but went and stood by him.
sentences.n: οὐδ’ ἄρ’ ἔτι δήν 'and not for long any more' means that Telemachus did not stay apart for long. ἑκάς 'away' takes the genitive ξείνοιο, a genitive in -οιο of ξεῖνος. τράπετ’ is τράπετο, an unaugmented aorist middle of τρέπω, 'turned himself'. παρέστη is the aorist of παρίστημι, 'stood beside', and the contrast is made with ἀλλά.

sentences.t: τὸν καὶ Πείραιος πρότερος πρὸς μῦθον ἔειπε·
sentences.l: Him also Peiraeus, first, with a word addressed:
sentences.i: Peiraeus spoke to him first, with these words:
sentences.n: τὸν is 'him', Telemachus. πρὸς … ἔειπε is a tmesis, a split form of προσέειπε 'spoke to, addressed', with ἔειπε the aorist of the root of εἶπον, and μῦθον 'a word' stands between the two halves. πρότερος is a comparative that English turns into an adverb, 'first', and καί is 'also'; with πρότερος it says that Peiraeus was the first to speak to him.

sentences.t:
Τηλέμαχ’, αἶψ’ ὄτρυνον ἐμὸν ποτὶ δῶμα γυναῖκας,
ὥς τοι δῶρ’ ἀποπέμψω, ἅ τοι Μενέλαος ἔδωκε.
sentences.l:
“Telemachus, quickly urge on to my house women,
so that to you the gifts I may send off, which to you Menelaus gave.”
sentences.i: “Telemachus, send women to my house at once, so that I may send you the gifts that Menelaus gave you.”
sentences.n: ὄτρυνον is the imperative of ὀτρύνω 'urge on, speed on its way'; the women are to be sent to Peiraeus' house, and the next line gives the reason, so the sense is that they will fetch the gifts. ποτί is πρός 'to'. ὥς is ὡς 'so that', accented because τοι follows it, and ἀποπέμψω is a purpose subjunctive. τοι 'to you' stands twice in the two lines. The gifts are those that Menelaus gave Telemachus.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖ Τηλέμαχος πεπνυμένος ἀντίον ηὔδα·
sentences.l: To him in turn prudent Telemachus spoke, face to face:
sentences.i: Then prudent Telemachus spoke to him in turn, face to face:
sentences.n: The same line as 45, with τόν for τήν because the person addressed is now a man, Peiraeus: τὸν δ’ αὖ is 'and him in turn'. πεπνυμένος 'prudent' and ἀντίον ηὔδα 'spoke face to face' are the same words as before, and so is the English.

sentences.t: Πείραι’, οὐ γάρ τ’ ἴδμεν ὅπως ἔσται τάδε ἔργα.
sentences.l: “Peiraeus, for we do not know how these deeds will be.
sentences.i: “Peiraeus, we cannot tell how these matters will turn out.
sentences.n: Πείραι’ is the vocative of Πείραιος, elided. οὐ γάρ τ’ ἴδμεν is 'for we do not know': ἴδμεν is the Homeric form of ἴσμεν, 'we know', and γάρ introduces the reason for what he goes on to say. The epic τε follows γάρ. ὅπως ἔσται opens an indirect question, and τάδε ἔργα 'these deeds', a neuter plural, has a singular verb. This sentence gives the reason for what follows: Telemachus cannot yet tell how things will go, so he sets out two cases.

sentences.t:
εἴ κεν ἐμὲ μνηστῆρες ἀγήνορες ἐν μεγάροισι
λάθρη κτείναντες πατρώϊα πάντα δάσωνται,
αὐτὸν ἔχοντά σε βούλομ’ ἐπαυρέμεν, ἤ τινα τῶνδε·
sentences.i: if the lordly suitors kill me secretly in the halls and divide all my father’s goods among themselves, I would rather you yourself had them and enjoyed them than any one of these men;
sentences.n: εἴ κεν with the subjunctive δάσωνται, from δατέομαι 'divide', makes a possible case, 'if they should share out'. ἐμέ is the object of the aorist participle κτείναντες 'having killed', which comes first in time. πατρώϊα is 'what belonged to my father'. αὐτὸν ἔχοντά σε is 'you yourself having (them)', and βούλομ’ ἐπαυρέμεν 'I wish to enjoy' (ἐπαυρέμεν is an infinitive in -έμεν); ἤ is 'rather than'. τῶνδε 'of these' means the suitors.

sentences.t:
εἰ δέ κ’ ἐγὼ τούτοισι φόνον καὶ κῆρα φυτεύσω,
δὴ τότε μοι χαίροντι φέρειν πρὸς δώματα χαίρων.
sentences.l:
but if I for these men murder and doom shall plant,
then indeed to me rejoicing to bring them to the house, rejoicing.”
sentences.i: But if I sow death and doom for these men, then bring them to the house, glad as I shall be, and glad yourself.”
sentences.n: φυτεύσω 'I plant' is the verb of line 27, where the poet said that Telemachus was planting evils for the suitors. φόνον and κῆρα are 'murder' and 'doom'; κῆρα is from κήρ 'doom, death' (a different word from κῆρ 'heart'). δὴ τότε is 'then indeed'. φέρειν 'to bring' is an infinitive used as an order, with the gifts understood. μοι χαίροντι is 'to me rejoicing' and χαίρων is Peiraeus 'rejoicing': both are to be glad.

sentences.t: ὣς εἰπὼν ξεῖνον ταλαπείριον ἦγεν ἐς οἶκον.
sentences.l: So having spoken, the stranger, much-tried, he led to his house.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and led the stranger, much tried as he was, to his house.
sentences.n: ὣς εἰπών is 'so having spoken', and the subject is Telemachus. ταλαπείριος is 'much-tried', a compound of the root of τλάω 'endure' and πεῖρα 'trial', and is translated though the stranger has only just come. ἦγεν is the imperfect of ἄγω, 'was leading, led'. ἐς οἶκον is 'to the house'. Murray begins a new paragraph here.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεί ῥ’ ἵκοντο δόμους εὖ ναιετάοντας,
χλαίνας μὲν κατέθεντο κατὰ κλισμούς τε θρόνους τε,
ἐς δ’ ἀσαμίνθους βάντες ἐϋξέστας λούσαντο.
sentences.l:
But when they reached the well-inhabited house,
cloaks, on the one hand, they laid down on seats and chairs,
and into baths having gone, well-polished, they bathed.
sentences.i: When they reached the well-inhabited house, they laid their cloaks down on seats and chairs, and went into the well-polished baths and bathed.
sentences.n: Line 85 repeats the formula of line 28, with ἵκοντο 'they reached' for ἵκανε. χλαῖνα is a 'cloak', and κατὰ … κλισμούς is 'down on seats'; κλισμός is a seat to lean back in (from κλίνω), θρόνος a 'chair'. ἀσάμινθος is a 'bath'. ἐϋξέστας is 'well-polished'. βάντες 'having gone' is the aorist participle of βαίνω; λούσαντο 'they bathed' is the middle aorist of λούω.

sentences.t:
τοὺς δ’ ἐπεὶ οὖν δμῳαὶ λοῦσαν καὶ χρῖσαν ἐλαίῳ,
ἀμφὶ δ’ ἄρα χλαίνας οὔλας βάλον ἠδὲ χιτῶνας,
ἔκ ῥ’ ἀσαμίνθων βάντες ἐπὶ κλισμοῖσι καθῖζον.
sentences.l:
And them, when then the slave-women had bathed and anointed with oil,
and about them had thrown thick cloaks and tunics,
out of the baths they stepped and on seats sat down.
sentences.i: And when the serving-women had bathed and anointed them with oil, and put thick cloaks and tunics about them, they stepped out of the baths and sat down on seats.
sentences.n: τοὺς δ’ is 'and them', object of λοῦσαν and χρῖσαν, which are unaugmented aorists. ἐπεὶ οὖν is 'when then'. Lines 88–89 are 4.49–50, shipped in odyssey-014, and that English is kept word for word, so δμῳαί is 'slave-women' here (and 'serving-women' in i); at line 34, where no earlier line binds the wording, it is 'maidservants'. ἀμφὶ … βάλον is tmesis, 'threw about', and οὔλας is 'thick, woolly', said of cloaks. ἔκ ῥ’ ἀσαμίνθων is 'out of the baths', and καθῖζον is the imperfect of καθίζω 'sit down', which takes ἐπὶ κλισμοῖσι 'on seats'.

sentences.t:
χέρνιβα δ’ ἀμφίπολος προχόῳ ἐπέχευε φέρουσα
καλῇ χρυσείῃ, ὑπὲρ ἀργυρέοιο λέβητος,
νίψασθαι·
sentences.i: A handmaid brought water for the hands in a fine golden pitcher and poured it over a silver basin, for them to wash;
sentences.n: χέρνιβα is water for washing the hands, and it is poured from the pitcher, προχόῳ, over a basin to catch it. ἀμφίπολος is a handmaid who attends; ἀργυρέοιο λέβητος is a genitive in -οιο after ὑπέρ, 'over a silver basin'. χρυσείῃ is 'golden'. νίψασθαι is an aorist middle infinitive of νίζω, 'for washing', and gives the purpose of the pouring.

sentences.t: παρὰ δὲ ξεστὴν ἐτάνυσσε τράπεζαν.
sentences.l: and beside them she drew up a polished table.
sentences.i: and she drew a polished table up beside them.
sentences.n: παρὰ … ἐτάνυσσε is tmesis, with δέ in between, 'stretched out beside'; the verb is τανύω 'stretch', and the handmaid is its subject. ξεστήν is 'polished', the adjective of which ἐϋξέστας in line 87 is the intensified form. τράπεζα is a table.

sentences.t:
σῖτον δ’ αἰδοίη ταμίη παρέθηκε φέρουσα,
εἴδατα πόλλ’ ἐπιθεῖσα, χαριζομένη παρεόντων.
sentences.l:
And bread a revered housekeeper set beside them, bringing it,
and laid on many dishes, giving freely of what was at hand;
sentences.i: A revered housekeeper brought bread and set it beside them, and laid on many dishes, giving freely of what she had by her;
sentences.n: ταμίη is the housekeeper in charge of the stores, and αἰδοίη 'revered' is her stock epithet, translated every time. σῖτον is 'bread, food'. παρέθηκε is the aorist of παρατίθημι, 'set beside'. εἴδατα are 'dishes, things to eat'. χαριζομένη παρεόντων is 'giving freely of what was there': παρεόντων is a genitive participle of πάρειμι, and the genitive is partitive after 'giving freely'.

sentences.t:
μήτηρ δ’ ἀντίον ἷζε παρὰ σταθμὸν μεγάροιο
κλισμῷ κεκλιμένη, λέπτ’ ἠλάκατα στρωφῶσα.
sentences.l:
And his mother opposite sat, beside a post of the hall,
reclining on a seat, fine yarn turning.
sentences.i: His mother sat opposite them, beside a post of the hall, leaning back on a seat and twirling fine yarn.
sentences.n: ἀντίον 'opposite' is an adverb, and ἷζε is the imperfect of ἵζω 'sit'. σταθμός is 'post', the same noun that earlier meant the steading; whether a doorpost or pillar of the hall is not said. κλισμῷ κεκλιμένη plays on one root: the seat is the one you lean back in, and κεκλιμένη is a perfect participle of κλίνω 'lean'. λέπτ’ is λεπτά 'fine'; ἠλάκατα, related to ἠλακάτη 'distaff', is 'yarn', the spun wool, and στρωφῶσα is 'turning, twirling'.

sentences.t:
οἱ δ’ ἐπ’ ὀνείαθ’ ἑτοῖμα προκείμενα χεῖρας ἴαλλον,
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ πόσιος καὶ ἐδητύος ἐξ ἔρον ἕντο,
τοῖσι δὲ μύθων ἦρχε περίφρων Πηνελόπεια·
sentences.l:
And they to the good things ready and set before them put out their hands,
but when of drink and of food they had put away desire,
and among them of speeches made-beginning circumspect Penelope:
sentences.i: And they put out their hands to the good things lying ready before them; and when they had put from them the desire for drink and food, circumspect Penelope was the first to speak among them:
sentences.n: The first line is the formula for taking food: ὀνείατα 'good things' are the dishes, ἑτοῖμα 'ready' and προκείμενα 'set out before them' agree with it. The second line is the formula for the end of a meal: ἐξ … ἕντο is a tmesis of ἐξίημι 'put away', so they 'put away' the desire for drink and food, both genitives. τοῖσι is 'among them', and μύθων ἦρχε is 'began the talk', ἄρχω taking the genitive. Penelope's speech begins after this unit.
